entries.section: 1. A call to his people to seek righteousness:

paragraphs.text: 1 Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together, O nation not desired; 2 Before the decree bring forth, before the day pass as the chaff, before the fierce anger of the LORD come upon you, before the day of the LORD’s anger come upon you. 3 Seek ye the LORD, all ye meek of the earth, which have wrought his judgment; seek righteousness, seek meekness: it may be ye shall be hid in the day of the LORD’s anger.

Before He begins to judge the nations that gloat over His people who are under discipline, He asks His people to repent and to seek righteousness and humility, so that the Lord may cover them and restore their glory to them. He does not judge those who gloat over His people unless the latter offer sincere repentance.
Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together, O nation not desired. [1]

He calls this nation, which considered itself God’s people, distinguished from the rest of the nations and peoples, to review its position, for it is a “nation not desired,” or “a nation not desiring God,” or one that has nothing to commend it before Him. He asks it to gather itself and to gather together, for one of the grave fruits of sin is the loss of the common purpose, so that each one acts according to his own whim. As it was said of the dark period of the Judges: “In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes” (Judg 21:25).
Sin makes a person like chaff that has no place of rest, and turns society into a storm that scatters and disperses everyone.

On the contrary, the work of true repentance is the return of a person to his depths, to look by the Spirit of truth into his heart, his thought, his feelings, his intentions and his will… Here he cleaves to God, and so draws near to his brethren in the spirit of unity, not by mere bodily gathering, but so that all have one Spirit and one mind.

Here the call to gather with her is perhaps so that all may review their accounts together, offer a communal repentance, and turn away from themselves the shame and the divine wrath, in a spirit of prayer, reverence and desire to return to Him.
Before the decree bring forth.
Before the day pass as the chaff.
Before the fierce anger of the LORD come upon you.

entries.section: 1. A call to his people to seek righteousness:

paragraphs.text: Before the day of the LORD’s anger come upon you. [2]
If His people have fallen under discipline, He warns them that unless they return to Him they will fall under the divine wrath in the day of the LORD’s anger.

If sin corrupts people’s lives and makes of them straw rather than wheat, then the slightest attack of an enemy becomes like the wind, and the straw is scattered and dispersed. But repentance makes wheat of the straw, so that the winds do not scatter them, but rather cleanse them of the straw so that the wheat is gathered together.
He asks them for swift and zealous repentance, for the day of the birth of the decree, or the day of divine discipline, has drawn very near; it is at the doors.

Perhaps He likens the day of the Lord here to chaff, which comes swiftly when the winds of divine wrath blow; and when the day comes the wicked find no opportunity to flee, for it will pass like chaff that is hard to overtake, and they themselves become chaff in the blast of violent winds! As the psalmist says: “The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away” (Ps 1:4). And as the Lord says of the wicked people of Ephraim: “Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney” (Hos 13:3).
Thus the wicked find no place of rest; they do not settle upon the earth, nor do they reach heaven. They are like the storm that the wind drives in every direction.

St. Augustine compares the meek with the wicked. Of the meek it was said: “Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth” (Mt 5:5); but the wicked are like dust (and ashes) that the wind drives away from the face of the earth (Ps 1:4). For pride puffs up the wicked man, so that he is always driven away from the face of the earth.

* The wicked are “like the chaff which the wind driveth away” (Ps 1:4). Scripture says that the wicked man is unhappy, so that he is not even like the dust of the earth. Dust appears as though it had no being, yet it has a kind of existence in itself… It is scattered here and there and has no place in which to settle; wherever the wind sweeps it, its strength is dissipated. So is the wicked man: since he denies God, he is led by error, wherever the breezes of the devil send him.

St. Jerome * “Let them be as chaff before the wind: and let the angel of the LORD chase them” (Ps 35:5)… The wind is temptation, and the dust (the chaff) is the wicked. When temptation comes the dust rises and does not stand before the wind nor resist it.
St. Augustine Seek ye the LORD, all ye meek of the earth, which have wrought his judgment;
Seek righteousness,
Seek meekness.

entries.section: 1. A call to his people to seek righteousness:

paragraphs.text: It may be ye shall be hid in the day of the LORD’s anger. [3]

In calling them to gather together He did not wish each of them to instill in the other a spirit of terror and dread, but that they gather together to seek the Lord. They seek the Lord that He may pour out His grace upon them and have mercy on them, and fulfill His promises to them. He calls them to gather in a spirit of gentleness, like sick people asking the heavenly Physician to stretch out His hand to treat and heal. Therefore He calls them: “all ye wretched (meek) of the earth.”

It is remarkable that He calls the meek of the earth (the wretched of the earth) to seek the Lord Himself and to ask Him for righteousness and humility; by this they are hidden in the day of the LORD’s anger. There is no way to hide from wrath except by taking refuge in the Lord and hiding in Him, and enjoying the divine righteousness, which covers their weaknesses, and obtaining humility, so that they become wheat instead of being chaff in the blast of the raging wind.

The Lord proclaimed this same call in the book of Isaiah: “Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast. For, behold, the LORD cometh out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity” (Isa 26:20-21). And in Amos: “For thus saith the LORD unto the house of Israel, Seek ye me, and ye shall live… Seek the LORD, and ye shall live; lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph, and devour it, and there be none to quench it in Beth-el” (Amos 5:4, 6).

Some see that the address here is directed to the class of the wretched who fell under oppression because of the corruption that had come upon the land, and the exploitation of the opportunity against the poor by the powerful and the rich. Yet these poor also shared in the corruption and the abominations; therefore the prophet asks them to return to the Lord and seek His mercy by repentance in humility and by walking in righteousness. For the oppression that has come upon them will not justify them on the day of the LORD’s anger unless they return to Him with all their hearts.

Perhaps he means by the wretched here the Jews who crucified Christ; if they blasphemed Him and crucified Him, let them recognize Him and seek Him in a spirit of humility, and He will embrace them and keep them from the wrath that came upon them because of their denial of Him. For it was said to them by the prophet Isaiah: “Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near” (Isa 55:6).

St. Cyprian sees in the call “Seek the Lord” an invitation to leave everything in order to seek the Lord and His Kingdom and His righteousness, and then everything will be added to us, as the Lord Christ Himself said (Mt 6:31-33).

* While there is time, look to true and eternal salvation, and since the end of the world is at the doors, turn your minds in the fear of the Lord to God. Do not rejoice in your vain authority, which without power rules in this world over the righteous and the meek… “Seek the LORD, and ye shall live” (Amos 5:6). Know the Lord, even if the time is late… Believe in Him, who will not deceive you. Believe in Him who foretold to you the coming of all these things. Believe in Him who will give eternal life to those who believe. Believe in Him who by the fires of hell will inflict eternal punishment on those who do not believe.
The martyr Cyprian Thus we have no refuge from the wrath of the Lord except fleeing to Him and taking shelter in Him.
* Before we sought the Lord we were weak and unstable; now that our hearts are settled upon Him we are strong and courageous.
St. Jerome

4 For Gaza shall be forsaken, and Ashkelon a desolation: they shall drive out Ashdod at the noon day, and Ekron shall be rooted up. 5 Woe unto the inhabitants of the sea coast, the nation of the Cherethites! the word of the LORD is against you; O Canaan, the land of the Philistines, I will even destroy thee, that there shall be no inhabitant. 6 And the sea coast shall be dwellings and cottages for shepherds, and folds for flocks. 7 And the coast shall be for the remnant of the house of Judah; they shall feed thereupon: in the houses of Ashkelon shall they lie down in the evening: for the LORD their God shall visit them, and turn away their captivity.
For Gaza shall be forsaken, and Ashkelon a desolation.
They shall drive out Ashdod at the noon day, and Ekron shall be rooted up. [4]

The Lord disciplines the important cities of Philistia, which prided themselves in arrogance upon their power or prosperity, namely Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod and Ekron. The city of Gaza becomes forsaken, like a barren wilderness; Alexander the Great destroyed it completely, so that he almost erased it. Its name in Hebrew came as “deceitful, Gazubah,” which carries this meaning, that is, without existence. As for the second city, Ashkelon, in Hebrew it is Ekron teeaker.

Ashdod is driven out at the time of noon. The Easterners have known from ancient times that they sleep at noon because of the heat, so it is considered a time of idleness (2 Sam 4:5), and military operations used to stop during that period.

It is noted that the fifth well-known city of Philistia, “Gath,” is not mentioned here because at that time it was subject to the Jews. For this reason Zephaniah here, and Amos (Amos 1:6), Jeremiah (Jer 25:20) and Zechariah (Zech 9:5-6) mentioned only the four cities.

What he prophesies here concerning these four principal cities points to what befalls the wicked, unrepentant man, namely that he suffers isolation, being forsaken; desolation, where the divine righteousness does not dwell in him; terror, where he lives as a fugitive with none pursuing him; and finally being rooted up, where his life ends with the fate of the enemy of good himself.

This is the divine warning to every man who chooses for himself to resist the divine truth and to turn his back on God, the Giver of life, satisfaction, peace and happiness. He groans with Zion, who in her bitterness thought that the Lord had forsaken her and her Lord had forgotten her (Isa 49:14), and says: “Behold, I was left alone” (Isa 49:21). And as the prophet Jeremiah says: “Every city shall be forsaken, and not a man dwell therein” (Jer 4:29). As was said by the prophet Isaiah: “And they shall look unto the earth; and behold trouble and darkness, dimness of anguish; and they shall be driven to darkness” (Isa 8:22). And as was said by the psalmist: “Let their habitation be desolate; and let none dwell in their tents” (Ps 69:25); “How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment!” (Ps 73:19). And it is said in the Maccabees: “He rooted out every wicked and evil man” (1 Macc 14:14).

* “How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment!” (Ps 73:19) He marvels at them, perceiving what will finally befall them. “They have vanished”; truly they have become like smoke, which, as it ascends on high, vanishes; so have they vanished… “They are consumed by their iniquities.” They are like a dream when one awaketh (Ps 73:20)… When a man sees that he has found treasures while he sleeps, he is only under the illusion that he is rich, but until he awakes… he searches and does not find; there is nothing in his hands, nothing in his bed… These (the wicked), when they awake, find the misery that they prepared for themselves.

St. Augustine If evil demolishes a person and robs him of all vitality, so that he is like one abandoned in isolation, destruction comes upon him and he is rooted up, then God who permits this does so in order to root out the evil in him and to plant him anew, that is, to renew his life and nature by His Holy Spirit. He shatters the evil in us in order to establish His righteousness in us. As the psalmist says: “Thou with thy hand hast rooted out the nations, and planted them” (Ps 44:2).
Woe unto the inhabitants of the sea coast, the nation of the Cherethites.
The word of the LORD is against you; O Canaan, the land of the Philistines, I will even destroy thee, that there shall be no inhabitant. [5]
By the sea coast is meant the whole region on the shore of the Mediterranean Sea from Egypt to Joppa and Gaza. The Hebrew word is Ceroth, which corresponds in sound to “water basins, dug cisterns.”
And the sea coast shall be dwellings and cottages for shepherds, and folds for flocks. [6]

The sea coast, which was used as a harbor for ships and inhabited by merchants, becomes empty of inhabitants. It is transformed from a commercial land full of activity and vitality into a pasture for sheep and folds.

Some see that by the nation of the Cherethites is meant a group of sojourners or immigrants from Phoenicia, mentioned in (1 Sam 30:14; Amos 9:7). In the Septuagint and the Syriac it appears under the name “Crete.”
And the coast shall be for the remnant of the house of Judah.
They shall feed thereupon.
In the houses of Ashkelon shall they lie down in the evening: for the LORD their God shall visit them, and turn away their captivity. [7]
He prophesies here that the house of Judah will regain its possession of Ashkelon, and that the remnant returning from captivity will settle in safety in the houses of Ashkelon.

Alexander the Great destroyed Ashkelon, and the Maccabees fulfilled what the prophets had prophesied against it, as it lost its system of government completely, and the people were finally compelled to be circumcised, that is, to enter Judaism by force.

entries.section: 3. The judgment of Moab and Ammon:

paragraphs.text: 8 I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the revilings of the children of Ammon, whereby they have reproached my people, and magnified themselves against their border. 9 Therefore as I live, saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation: the residue of my people shall spoil them, and the remnant of my people shall possess them. 10 This shall they have for their pride, because they have reproached and magnified themselves against the people of the LORD of hosts. 11 The LORD will be terrible unto them: for he will famish all the gods of the earth; and men shall worship him, every one from his place, even all the isles of the heathen.
I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the revilings of the children of Ammon, whereby they have reproached my people, and magnified themselves against their border. [8]

The sons of Moab and the sons of Ammon are linked together, for each of Moab and Ammon is an illegitimate son of the fallen Lot (Gen 19:33-38). These two peoples represent those who are bastards and not children of God, for they refuse to believe in the Lord Christ and do not enjoy the new spiritual birth.

The sons of Moab and the sons of Ammon fell under discipline because they mocked the Jewish people during their discipline and blasphemed their God. In their mockery and gloating over them they thought that the God of Israel did not hear and had no power to resist them; therefore He says: “I have heard the reproach of Moab and the revilings of the children of Ammon,” even though in His long-suffering He seemed as one who does not hear until He disciplines His people.
“Magnified themselves against their border”: in arrogance and pride they raided the borders of Judah (Jer 48:29; 49:1).

Therefore as I live, saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation.

entries.section: 3. The judgment of Moab and Ammon:

paragraphs.text: The residue of my people shall spoil them, and the remnant of my people shall possess them. [9]

The fate of the Moabites and the Ammonites becomes like the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah, where every remembrance of them comes to an end, and their lands are turned into a desolation without inhabitant. Their land produces nettles, a plant with thorny hairs, instead of wheat, and their springs produce exceedingly salty waters instead of springs of sweet water, and they become spoil for Israel.

entries.section: 3. The judgment of Moab and Ammon:

paragraphs.text: This shall they have for their pride, because they have reproached and magnified themselves against the people of the LORD of hosts. [10]
What comes upon them is not arbitrary; rather it is the natural fruit of their pride and their arrogance against the people of the LORD of hosts.

entries.section: 3. The judgment of Moab and Ammon:

paragraphs.text: The LORD will be terrible unto them: for he will famish all the gods of the earth; and men shall worship him, every one from his place, even all the isles of the heathen. [11]

God affirms that there is no enmity in the heart of God toward any particular people or nation; rather the proud and blaspheming people fall under the yoke of their pride, blasphemy and evil. But God shatters the idols and raises up from all the nations a people for Himself, in which every nation worships Him, indeed every man in his place. There is no need for all to go up to Jerusalem and worship in the temple of Solomon.
This is what God was preparing His ancient people to accept, namely that the earth and the fullness thereof become the Lord’s and His Christ’s.
“Sing unto God, ye kingdoms of the earth; O sing praises unto the Lord; Selah” (Ps 68:32).
“And the LORD shall be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know the LORD in that day, and shall do sacrifice and oblation; yea, they shall vow a vow unto the LORD, and perform it” (Isa 19:21).

“For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering…” (Mal 1:11).

He lowers the standing of the pagan gods, so that they become exceedingly lean, like predatory beasts that have grown very lean for lack of food for a long time. No sacrifice is offered to them any more, nor is any worship offered in their temples.

* Let us now hear another prophet who presents the same prophecy, saying that the worship of God will no longer be limited to one place, but the time will come when every man will know Him. He is Zephaniah, who says: “The Lord will appear to all the nations, and will famish all the gods of the nations; then every one will worship Him from his place” (Zeph 2:11) LXX. However, this was forbidden to the Jews, since Moses commanded them to worship in one place.

* You hear that the prophets declared beforehand, prophesying that men will no longer be limited to a place, coming from all the earth to offer sacrifice in one city (or one place), but each one will remain in his house (his homeland) and serve God and honor Him. What time is like the present time in which it has been possible for these prophecies to be fulfilled? In any case, listen and understand how the Gospels and the Apostle Paul agree with Zephaniah. The prophet said: “The Lord will appear,” and Paul said: “For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all the people” (Titus 2:11). Zephaniah said: “to all the nations,” and Paul said: “to all men” (Titus 2:11). Zephaniah said: “He will famish your gods,” and Paul said: “Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world” (Titus 2:12).

St. John Chrysostom * You do not believe that it was foretold to us that these nations would come to a place of God, as it was said: “Unto thee shall the Gentiles come from the ends of the earth” (Jer 16:19). Understand, if you can, that the peoples of these nations come to the God of the Christians, who is the true Most High God, not by walking but by faith. For this very declaration was presented in these words by another prophet: “The LORD will be terrible unto them: for he will famish all the gods of the earth; and men shall worship him, every one from his place, even all the isles of the heathen” (Zeph 2:11). One prophet says: “Unto thee shall the Gentiles come from the ends of the earth,” and the other says: “Every one shall worship him from his place.” Therefore they are not required to withdraw from their places in order to come to Him, since they find Him, whom they believe, in their hearts.
* They will come to Him without leaving their places, for by faith in Him they find Him in their hearts.

* For a long time… the demons kept silence in their temples concerning the things that were to happen, although it was not possible for them to be without knowledge of them, because of the utterances of the prophets. But recently, as the events began to draw near, the demons wished to announce them beforehand, so that they might not appear ignorant or defeated. Yet they did not point to certain things that had been announced beforehand and recorded long ago, such as those found in the prophet Zephaniah: “The Lord will overcome them and drive out all the gods of the nations from the earth. And every man will worship Him from his place, all the isles of the nations” (Zeph 2:11). Perhaps those gods who were worshipped in the temples of the nations did not believe that these events would be fulfilled with regard to them, and therefore did not wish to cause irritation among the seers and diviners, the soothsayers who followed them.

St. Augustine * Let us speak also of the churches as islands. Add to this that Scripture says in another place: “Many islands have returned to me” (Isa 42:10) LXX. The prophet Isaiah says in the name of the Lord: “Speak to the inhabitants of this island,” “Let many islands rejoice.” Just as islands stand in the midst of the sea, so churches are established in the midst of the world, and are beaten and struck by many waves of persecutions. Truly these islands are tossed by the waves every day, but they are not overwhelmed by the waters. Surely they are in the midst of the sea, but their foundation is Christ, Christ who cannot be shaken.

St. Jerome * Despite all this, they were still unable to rebuild the temple and restore the place in which they were permitted to practice their rites according to the Law. For the authority of Christ, the authority that founded the Church, destroyed that place. The prophet had foretold that Christ would come, though He would not come except after the captivity.
St. John Chrysostom
Ye Ethiopians also.
Ye shall be slain by my sword. [12]
Nebuchadnezzar subdued Cush (Jer 46:9-10; Ezek 30:4). The Lord says: “my sword,” and means by it Nebuchadnezzar, whom God used as an instrument in His hand for disciplining the nations.

13 And he will stretch out his hand against the north, and destroy Assyria; and will make Nineveh a desolation, and dry like a wilderness. 14 And flocks shall lie down in the midst of her, all the beasts of the nations: both the cormorant and the bittern shall lodge in the upper lintels of it; a voice shall croak in the windows; desolation shall be in the thresholds: for her cedar work is laid bare. 15 This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me: how is she become a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in! every one that passeth by her shall hiss, and wag his hand.
And he will stretch out his hand against the north, and destroy Assyria; and will make Nineveh a desolation, and dry like a wilderness. [13]
The Lord destroyed the Assyrian Empire and made its capital, “Nineveh,” a desolation.
And flocks shall lie down in the midst of her, all the beasts of the nations.
Both the cormorant and the bittern shall lodge in the upper lintels of it.
A voice shall croak in the windows.
Desolation shall be in the thresholds.
For her cedar work is laid bare. [14]

Assyria is transformed from a great empire feared by all the nations of the world into wide wildernesses in which are found all kinds of animals, that is, domestic animals such as sheep, and predatory beasts. They become pastures without a law to govern them and without walls to protect the flocks. Its constitution becomes predation and death! As for birds, there is none in it except those that the Easterners considered gloomy birds, whose voices bring depression, sorrow and gloom, like the cormorant. Its birds do not know joyful songs but wailing in the windows.

When ruin and destruction come, the windows of the palaces stand open, and the birds perch on them mourning and lamenting. By the forces of nature the ceilings of the palaces, made of cedar wood as splendid works of art, are exposed, and these pieces lose their beauty and become a shelter for birds and insects. They become bare as the garment of their radiant beauty is stripped from them.

If Nineveh, the symbol of the wicked heart that is determined not to return to the Lord, has become a dwelling for the cormorant, which never ceases wailing and crying out, then the spiritual Jerusalem, the symbol of the holy heart, is a dwelling for the turtledove that rejoices continually. “The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land” (Song 2:12). It is as though the lot of the wicked is gloom full of despair, while the lot of the righteous is exultation full of hope. The heart of the wicked bears the earnest of hell, and the heart of the righteous bears the earnest of the eternal, heavenly, joyful Kingdom.

Assyria, which took Israel captive, was known for its extreme violence in dealing with captives. The kings found their delight in cutting off some members of the captives’ bodies, especially the rich and the nobles, and parading them in a mocking procession before the people; therefore it signifies the wicked, violent man, defiled with abominations. This state is turned into a lair of animals and none dwells in it except the cormorant and the hedgehog, and it becomes a desolation. But the holy soul becomes a joyful paradise full of the trees of virtue, and in it is heard the voice of the doves.
The following are the comments of St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, on what is said in the Song of Songs (Song 2:12).

* The echo of the voice makes the season delightful, and the singing of the birds resounds in the orchards, and the sweet echo of the turtledove’s voice reaches our ears… He has come who gave spring to our souls. He commanded the wind of evil that had stirred up the sea to be still: “And he said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm” (Mk 4:39). So everything became calm and our life began to flourish and was adorned with buds and flowers, and the flowers represent the virtue in our life that bears fruit in its seasons. Therefore the Word of God says: “For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; the flowers appear on the earth; the time of pruning is come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land” (Song 2:11-12)…

The Bridegroom says: “Behold, the meadows are flourishing with the flowers of virtue. Do you see this purity in the beauty of the fragrant narcissus? Do you see the rose of humility and the violet, which represents the sweet fragrance of the Lord Christ? Why, then, do you not make a crown of these flowers? For this is the season for cutting the flowers! And you make a branch into a crown to adorn yourself? The season of pruning has come. The voice of the turtledove bears witness to this; it resembles ‘the voice of one crying in the wilderness’ (Mt 3:3), for John the Baptist is the turtledove. He is the one who went before this luminous spring, who brought forth for the sons of men the wonderful flowers for cutting, and offered them to everyone who desired to gather them. It is he who showed us ‘there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse’ (Isa 11:1), and he is ‘the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world’ (Jn 1:29). And it is he who showed us repentance from sin and life according to virtue. The text says: ‘The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land’: and it calls ‘O land’ of those who were condemned for their sin, those whom the Gospel calls the tax collectors and the harlots, who heard the voice of John the Baptist while the rest did not accept his teaching.”
St. Gregory of Nyssa This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart:
I am, and there is none beside me.
How is she become a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in!
Every one that passeth by her shall hiss, and wag his hand. [15]

Nineveh was a rejoicing city that many longed to behold; its circumference was 60 miles, and the height of its walls about 100 feet, and three chariots side by side could drive upon its walls, and 1,500 watchtowers rose upon the walls. It became a desolation, so that it became difficult for anyone to know its location.

In arrogance Nineveh, like Babylon afterward and other arrogant lands, thought that it was the mistress of the world. The Lord says in Isaiah: “Therefore hear now this, thou that art given to pleasures, that dwellest carelessly, that sayest in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me; I shall not sit as a widow, neither shall I know the loss of children: But these two things shall come to thee in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood” (Isa 47:8-9).

The city of Nineveh represents the soul that is self-reliant and self-sufficient, not in God, and so it amuses itself in the world and thinks that it is in peace and security, and that no one can stand before it.
May You shatter my evil, and establish Your righteousness in me!
* Let my soul gather together with the souls of all Your people.
Let us gather together by Your Holy Spirit.
Expose before my eyes my audacity and my arrogance.
Burn up all evil within me and in my conduct, and grant me Your righteousness as a covering for my depths.
* Sin has made me like chaff in the blast of the winds.
I cannot stand before Your wrath.
Who is justified before You, O Holy One?
Your fiery Spirit renews my nature and turns me from chaff into holy wheat!
* To You I flee, O Savior; You take away my misery and grant me Your mercy.
In place of my arrogance, You grant me Your gentleness and Your humility.
You are my fortress; in You I hide, and You cover my weakness.
* Remove from within me every trace of idolatry.
Shatter every image I have set up for myself in my foolishness.
And may You take possession of all my heart and my being.
Without You my soul becomes forsaken, abandoned and desolate.
Without You all life in me is rooted up.
Enter into my depths, and establish Your heavenly Kingdom.
So that I no longer become a wasteland, a pasture for sheep.
Let the voice of the turtledove be heard within me, singing and praising Your name.
And let there be no place within me for the cormorant and other crying birds.
Let no voice of wailing be heard, but exultation and joy.
* Reveal Yourself within me in the splendor of Your glory.
So that all pride and arrogance flee from within me.
I will not judge anyone, but I will judge myself.
And I will not gloat over those who are under discipline, for I am deserving of every punishment, even death!
* By Your passing into my depths You open my insight, and I see You, the Savior of the whole world.
I see all peoples and nations having rejected every idol, and gathered around You like a triumphant procession.
The unclean nations have become Your holy bride.
The peoples hostile to You have become the object of Your delight.
Your heavens rejoice and exult in the holy humanity in You.
